title: MLOps using vetiver
text:
Introduction
In this section, we will demonstrate how one may combine vetiver and plumber with Docker and Kubernetes to enable Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) practices. MLOps is the practice of combining machine learning (ML) development with software engineering and operational practices. It applies principles from DevOps—like continuous integration, continuous delivery (CI/CD), version control, and monitoring to the lifecycle of ML models to make ML systems reproducible, scalable, and reliable. Models can then be updated safely, deployed efficiently, and monitored for performance drift over time
As a reminder:

vetiver: For model versioning, sharing, and deployment
plumber: For creating light-weight web applications, and deploying models as microservices
pins: For uploading, downloading, and sharing resources.

We will elucidate upon Docker and Kubernetes in subsequent sections.
We first load all required dependencies.

Sys.setenv("S3_ENDPOINT_URL" = "http://127.0.0.1:9000")

box::use(../../R/proj_utils)
box::use(../../R/tidymodels_deployment)

box::use(
  dials[svm_margin, trees, penalty, mixture],
  readr[read_csv, read_file],
  tune[control_grid, extract_parameter_set_dials, .get_tune_metric_names, select_best],
  here[here],
  dplyr[mutate, bind_rows, arrange, select, pull],
  purrr[pluck],
  ranger[ranger],
  kernlab,
  rsample[initial_split, vfold_cv, training, testing],
  parsnip[rand_forest, svm_linear, boost_tree, set_engine, set_mode, linear_reg],
  recipes[recipe, update_role, step_zv, step_nzv, step_normalize, step_impute_knn, update, all_numeric, all_outcomes],
  yardstick[rmse, mae, metric_set, metrics],
  hardhat[tune], 
  htmlwidgets[saveWidget],
  ggplot2[ggplot, geom_point, labs, theme_minimal, aes, geom_ribbon],
  workflows[workflow, add_recipe, add_model, fit],
  workflowsets[workflow_set, option_add, option_add_parameters, workflow_map, fit_best, workflow_autoplot = autoplot],
  stacks[stacks, add_candidates, blend_predictions, fit_members],
  vetiver[vetiver_model, vetiver_pin_write, vetiver_api, vetiver_pin_read],
  pins[board_temp, board_local, board_s3, pin_write, pin_read, pin_upload, pin_download],
  paws.common,
  paws.storage,
  plotly[ggplotly],
  probably[int_conformal_split, cal_plot_regression],
  plumber[pr, pr_run],
  DALEX[feature_importance, model_profile, predict_profile, model_diagnostics],
  DALEXtra[explain_tidymodels],
  glmnet,
  zeallot[...],
  targets[tar_make]
)

source(here("R/probably_vetiver.R"))



Data
We will next load an example dataset. For this tutorial, we will use the mtcars dataset.

data("mtcars")
head(mtcars)

                   mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
Mazda RX4         21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
Datsun 710        22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6  258 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8  360 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
Valiant           18.1   6  225 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1


We will next perform a 80-20 train-test data split.

data_split <- mtcars |>
  initial_split(
    prop = 0.8
  )

data_train <- training(data_split)
data_test  <- testing(data_split)

head(data_train)

                   mpg cyl  disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
Chrysler Imperial 14.7   8 440.0 230 3.23 5.345 17.42  0  0    3    4
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6 258.0 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
Merc 450SLC       15.2   8 275.8 180 3.07 3.780 18.00  0  0    3    3
Maserati Bora     15.0   8 301.0 335 3.54 3.570 14.60  0  1    5    8
Merc 450SL        17.3   8 275.8 180 3.07 3.730 17.60  0  0    3    3
Duster 360        14.3   8 360.0 245 3.21 3.570 15.84  0  0    3    4


Next, we will create a data preprocessing recipe using the recipes package, which will:

Drop zero and near zero-variance columns.
Normalise all numeric columns using Z-standardisation.
Impute missing data using k nearest neighbor imputation.


training_recipe <- recipe(data_train) |>
  update_role(everything(), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(mpg, new_role = "outcome") |>
  step_zv() |>
  step_nzv() |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes()) |>
  step_impute_knn()



Training
We will train a simple random forest model with default settings using tidymodels:

rf_recipe <- rand_forest() |> 
  set_engine("ranger") |> 
  set_mode("regression") 

rf_workflow <- workflow() |> 
  add_recipe(training_recipe) |> 
  add_model(rf_recipe)

fit_rf <- fit(rf_workflow, data = data_train) 



Uncertainty Quantification
Most implementations of random forest do not produce prediction intervals out-of-the-box. We will use a non-parametric (no distributional assumptions) and model-agnostic approach to constructing prediction intervals via the probably package.

conformalised_rf <- int_conformal_split(fit_rf, data_train)
conformalised_rf$training <- data_train

We can view the predictions of the random forest model:








Figure 1: Predicted and observed Miles per Gallon for testing set using conformalised random forest (95% prediction intervals).




Most of the testing observations fall within the 95% prediction intervals, though the predicted Miles per Gallon for larger weights are quite poor.


Model versioning, sharing, and deployment
We will demonstrate how to perform model versioning, sharing, and deployment using a combination of pins, vetiver, and plumber. We’ll store everything in S3. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is cloud storage for files, called “objects”, organized in “buckets”. It offers scalable, secure, and flexible storage with features like versioning, encryption, and programmatic access via URLs or AWS tools. In this example, we will first specify our S3 bucket.

board <- board_s3(
  "data", 
  access_key = "user", 
  secret_access_key = "password", 
  region = "us-east-2", 
  endpoint = Sys.getenv("S3_ENDPOINT_URL") 
)

We will generate and save several plots for our random forest model to upload into an S3 bucket:






Plots






save_s3_plot <- function(p, object_name, model, board) {
  outfile <- paste0(object_name, ".html")

  p |> 
    ggplotly() |>
    saveWidget(file.path("/tmp", outfile))
    
  model <- proj_utils$model_s3_upload(
    model, board, Sys.getenv("S3_ENDPOINT_URL"), 
    "/tmp", outfile, object_name
  )
  model
}

conformalised_rf <- conformalised_rf |>
  predict(new_data = data_test, level = 0.95) |>
  mutate(mpg = data_test$mpg) |>
  cal_plot_regression(truth = mpg, estimate = .pred) |>
  save_s3_plot("conformal_rf_calibration", conformalised_rf, board)

conformal_explainer <- 
  explain_tidymodels(
    model = conformalised_rf,
    data = data_train |> select(-mpg), 
    y = data_train |>  pull(mpg),
    label = "conformal"
  )

conformalised_rf <- feature_importance(
  conformal_explainer,
  type = "variable_importance",
  n_sample = 1000
) |>
  plot() |> 
  save_s3_plot("conformal_rf_variable_importance", conformalised_rf, board)

conformalised_rf <- model_profile(
  conformal_explainer,
  type = "partial"
) |>
  plot() |> 
  save_s3_plot("conformal_rf_pdp", conformalised_rf, board)

conformalised_rf <- model_diagnostics(
  conformal_explainer
) |>
  plot(variable = "y_hat", yvariable = "residuals") |> 
  save_s3_plot("conformal_rf_residuals", conformalised_rf, board)




vetiver offers support for generating model cards from an RMD template file. We will store a rendered model card as an HTML file within an S3 bucket using pins:

conformalised_rf <- proj_utils$model_s3_upload(
  conformalised_rf, 
  board, 
  Sys.getenv("S3_ENDPOINT_URL"), 
  here("pages", "tidymodels_workshop", "cards"), 
  "card.html", 
  "random_forest_card",
  is_card = TRUE
)

We will save our random forest model to an S3 bucket using pins and vetiver.

v_model <- vetiver_model(conformalised_rf, "random_forest")
vetiver_pin_write(v_model, board = board)

We will next load and interact with the saved model locally using a plumber web application.

Sys.setenv("MODEL_CARD_NAME" = "random_forest_card")

loaded_v <- board |> 
  vetiver_pin_read("random_forest")

pr(here("app", "api", "plumber.R")) |>
  vetiver_api(loaded_v) |>
  pr_run(port = 8088)



Docker
Docker is a containerisation technology that allows developers to package an application along with all its dependencies, libraries, and configuration files into a single unit called a container. This ensures that the application runs consistently across different environments — whether on a developer’s laptop, a testing server, or a production cloud environment. Docker helps developers “build once, run anywhere” without worrying about environment mismatches.
Our objective is to package up our plumber web application and model within a Docker container for subsequent deployment. In brief:

We have a Dockerfile which contains a sequence of steps needed to build a Docker image. We copy our code from the R workshop repo into the Docker image (including the plumber web application code).
We define a pipeline that builds the Docker image and pushes it into a container repository.
Our stored image may be found in the GitHub container repository.
We can then pull down our stored image and instantiate a container to deploy our plumber web application, either using Docker directly or with a container orchestration platform such as Kubernetes.
Our model can then be loaded into the web application within the container via S3.



Kubernetes
Kubernetes is an open-source platform that automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerised applications, such as our deployed models.
It organizes containers into logical units called pods, schedules them across a cluster of machines, and handles networking, storage, and load balancing. This ensures that your applications run reliably even as demand changes or failures occur. Kubernetes also provides self-healing features, automatically restarting or rescheduling containers when they fail.
In brief:

Kubernetes will pull down our Docker image containing our plumber web application.
Kubernetes will then deploy our web application within a pod inside our Kubernetes cluster.
Our S3 server is also running on Kubernetes, allowing us to load our model and any other artifacts of interest.

We can next use a partial dependence plot (PDP) to visualise the effect of one or more features on Miles per Gallon for our model, while averaging out the effects of all other features.

Figure 3: Partial dependence plots for the AutoML model.




We see that smaller values of Displacement, Horsepower, and Weight typically have more Miles per Gallon. There is a similar trend for the number of Cylinders, with a drop-off at around 5 and 7 cylinders.

title: Machine Learning Workflow using H2O
text:
Residuals
We will next produce a residuals plot to determine how well the model predicted Miles per Gallon at different values.








Figure 4: Residual plot for the AutoML model.




We see an S-shaped curve, suggesting that there is bias in the predictions. There is evidence of over-prediction for Miles per Gallon between 10 and 17, and between 21 and 28. Conversely, there is evidence of under-prediction for Miles per Gallon over 28 and between 17 and 22.

title: Generalised Linear Madness
text:
Data and Methods
During my PhD, I measured the length and weight of ~3000 freshwater mussels (yes I’m that exciting!). I want to describe the relationship between length and weight between mussels collected inside macrophyte beds (aquatic plant beds: treatment) vs not (control) based on how the data was generated.
Although the length-weight relationship isn’t technically a temporal relationship (even I’m not going to measure ~3000 mussels repeatedly over time), substituting time for space (length) will allow us to fit a models that estimate the: a) maximum weight; and b) growth rate.
To examine the relationship between the length and weight of freshwater mussels, generalized (non-)linear models were performed in R (R Core Team 2022) using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017). Linear, Gompertz (modified), and Logistic models were fitted with treatment (none vs macrophyte) as a predictor variable. A Gamma distribution was selected for the response since weight has positive and continuous values. Models were compared using leave-one-out cross validation and model validation was performed using prior and posterior predictive checks, as well as effective samples sizes and r-hats (McElreath, 2020).






Data






df <- readr::read_csv(here("pages/stan_workshop/data/Mussel_df_15.01.20.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

df <- df %>% dplyr::select(c(Length,Height,Width,Weight,Treatment,Macrophyte,Site))

df <- df[complete.cases(df),]  # Select only complete cases

head(df)

  lprior += normal_lpdf(b_r | 0, 0.05)

  lprior += normal_lpdf(b_delay | 30, 2)
    - 2 * normal_lccdf(0 | 30, 2);
  lprior += gamma_lpdf(shape | 0.01, 0.01);
}
model {
  // likelihood including constants
  if (!prior_only) {
    // initialize linear predictor term
    vector[N] nlp_k = rep_vector(0.0, N);
    // initialize linear predictor term
    vector[N] nlp_r = rep_vector(0.0, N);
    // initialize linear predictor term
    vector[N] nlp_delay = rep_vector(0.0, N);

Introduction
In this section, we will demonstrate how one may combine vetiver and plumber with Docker and Kubernetes to enable Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) practices. MLOps is the practice of combining machine learning (ML) development with software engineering and operational practices. It applies principles from DevOps—like continuous integration, continuous delivery (CI/CD), version control, and monitoring to the lifecycle of ML models to make ML systems reproducible, scalable, and reliable. Models can then be updated safely, deployed efficiently, and monitored for performance drift over time
As a reminder:

vetiver: For model versioning, sharing, and deployment
plumber: For creating light-weight web applications, and deploying models as microservices
pins: For uploading, downloading, and sharing resources.

We will elucidate upon Docker and Kubernetes in subsequent sections.
We first load all required dependencies.

Model versioning, sharing, and deployment
We will demonstrate how to perform model versioning, sharing, and deployment using a combination of pins, vetiver, and plumber. We’ll store everything in S3. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is cloud storage for files, called “objects”, organized in “buckets”.   vetiver_pin_read("gompertz")

  vetiver_api(loaded_v) |>
  pr_run(port = 8088)



Docker
Docker is a containerisation technology that allows developers to package an application along with all its dependencies, libraries, and configuration files into a single unit called a container. This ensures that the application runs consistently across different environments — whether on a developer’s laptop, a testing server, or a production cloud environment. Docker helps developers “build once, run anywhere” without worrying about environment mismatches.
Our objective is to package up our plumber web application and model within a Docker container for subsequent deployment. In brief:

We have a Dockerfile which contains a sequence of steps needed to build a Docker image. We copy our code from the R workshop repo into the Docker image (including the plumber web application code).
We define a pipeline that builds the Docker image and pushes it into a container repository.
Our stored image may be found in the GitHub container repository.
We can then pull down our stored image and instantiate a container to deploy our plumber web application, either using Docker directly or with a container orchestration platform such as Kubernetes.
Our model can then be loaded into the web application within the container via S3.



Kubernetes
Kubernetes is an open-source platform that automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerised applications, such as our deployed models.
It organizes containers into logical units called pods, schedules them across a cluster of machines, and handles networking, storage, and load balancing. This ensures that your applications run reliably even as demand changes or failures occur. Kubernetes also provides self-healing features, automatically restarting or rescheduling containers when they fail.
In brief:

Kubernetes will pull down our Docker image containing our plumber web application.
Kubernetes will then deploy our web application within a pod inside our Kubernetes cluster.
Our S3 server is also running on Kubernetes, allowing us to load our model and any other artifacts of interest.

title: Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct
text:
We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.
We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.



Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
Public or private harassment
Publishing others’ private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting




Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.
Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.



This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.



Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at GitHub Issues. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.
All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.



Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:


Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.
Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.



Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.
Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.



Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.
Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.



Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.
Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.




This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.0, available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/0/code_of_conduct.html.
Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by Mozilla’s code of conduct enforcement ladder.
For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq. Translations are available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations.

title: Security Policy
text:
Security Policy
If you discover a security vulnerability in this project, we encourage you to let us know right away. Please report security issues to us by creating a new security advisory.
The following information will help us triage your report more quickly:

Type of issue (e.g. buffer overflow, SQL injection, cross-site scripting, etc.)
Full paths of source file(s) related to the manifestation of the issue
The location of the affected source code (tag/branch/commit or direct URL)
Any special configuration required to reproduce the issue
Step-by-step instructions to reproduce the issue
Proof-of-concept or exploit code (if possible)
Impact of the issue, including how an attacker might exploit the issue
